speaker: Moses Kagan
title: Repositioning 80 Apartment Buildings with Moses Kagan
question: In distressed multifamily real estate, how can a broker-operator monetize undervalued rehab deals they lack the capital to buy themselves?
guest: Twice a week people ask me how to build a first deal into a full-time business when you're only making $40K in fees and maybe $70K two years later, while you have kids and rent to pay. When we started, we didn't have any money. I had my brokerage license and my partner had his contractor's license. I built a business representing buyers, and the problem was I'd show them a beat-up building that was cheap per square foot, and they'd say, 'Congratulations, you found a cheap deal, but I don't have the first idea what to do with it or know any contractors.' So I brought my partner in for a consulting fee to oversee renovations, and we split the brokerage commission and construction fee. That evolved into a fee development business. There were good deals we didn't have the capital to buy ourselves, so we found clients willing to pay us $100K to $150K to run the whole process without us having ownership. Stacking those projects allowed us to live while building up our track record and the network of investors who ultimately capitalized our future deals.

points.core: Retail buyers often reject cheap distressed buildings because they lack renovation execution capability.
points.note: Accept: capitalized buyers passing on beat-up, undervalued properties because they lack contractor networks or construction management know-how. Do not credit: generic claims that distressed properties are 'risky' without pointing to the buyer's execution bottleneck.

points.core: Operators bundle buyer brokerage with construction oversight into a turnkey fee-development service.
points.note: Accept: pairing deal sourcing/brokerage with renovation management so third-party buyers can acquire and reposition heavy-rehab buildings end-to-end. Do not credit: merely brokering deals for a standard commission without adding construction/rehab execution.

points.core: Charging flat development fees without equity ownership monetizes deals despite lacking capital.
points.note: Accept: taking substantial fixed project fees (e.g., $100K–$150K) to execute rehabs for capitalized third-party owners instead of requiring principal equity. Do not credit: suggesting raising a fund or taking debt without addressing non-equity fee monetization.

points.core: Stacking third-party fee projects funds living expenses until an investor network matures.
points.note: Accept: layering multiple fee-development engagements covers immediate cash flow and builds track record/LP relationships for future principal syndications. Do not credit: generic advice to 'build a track record' without linking stacked fee projects to surviving the early income gap.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A broker-operator who finds deals but lacks capital can get paid for sourcing, structuring, and executing rather than for owning outright. The main route is to control the deal and bring in other people's money: put the property under contract, then syndicate or joint-venture it with capital partners. In return they typically take an acquisition fee, a promoted (carried) interest in the profits, and ongoing asset management, property management and construction management fees for running the rehab and lease-up. Their sweat equity and deal sourcing substitute for a cash contribution.

Simpler options trade upside for speed and lower risk. They can wholesale the deal by assigning the purchase contract to a better-capitalized buyer for an assignment fee, or do a double close. Or they can simply broker it, earning a commission and often negotiating to keep the management contract or the listing on the eventual resale.

A hybrid is common: accept a small co-GP stake in place of part of the fee.

One caution is that raising money from passive investors usually triggers securities law, and brokers must disclose any principal interest to clients.

points.why: The response never identifies buyers’ lack of renovation know-how or contractor relationships as a reason they pass on cheap distressed buildings.
The response places construction oversight within a syndication or joint venture and never bundles it with buyer representation as a turnkey service.
The response never proposes a fixed project fee for executing a rehab on behalf of a third-party owner without taking equity.
The response never connects stacking fee-development projects to covering living expenses while building a track record and investor relationships.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: A broker-operator can monetize undervalued multifamily rehab deals without personal capital by trading deal access, operational execution, and licensing across three primary structures. First, they can sponsor a joint venture or syndication as the general partner, pairing their sourcing and turnaround expertise with passive limited partners or a family office that funds the equity and rehab reserves. This structure generates upfront acquisition fees, ongoing construction and asset management fees, and a promoted share of profits upon refinance or sale, while rolling their buyer-side commission into the deal can satisfy GP co-investment requirements without out-of-pocket cash. Second, for immediate liquidity without project risk, they can place the distressed property under contract and assign the agreement—or double-close—to a capitalized buyer for a wholesale spread, taking care to satisfy mandatory broker license disclosures. Third, they can present the off-market deal to a funded investor in exchange for an acquisition commission bundled with contracts for renovation oversight, property management, and the exclusive disposition listing once stabilized, turning a single lead into recurring fee income and two brokerage commissions.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A broker-operator can make money on these deals in several ways while putting in little or no cash of their own.

**Assign the contract.** They can put the property under contract, then assign it to a well-funded buyer for a fee, or do a double close. This is the simplest route, but it pays only once.

**Partner with capital.** Usually the better route is a joint venture or syndication. Equity partners or family offices put up most of the money. The broker-operator sources the deal, runs the rehab and lease-up, and earns several kinds of pay:
- an acquisition fee (often 1–3%)
- construction-management and asset-management fees
- often in-house property management
- a "promote," meaning a disproportionate share of profits (commonly 20–30%) once investors hit a preferred return (the minimum return investors get before the sponsor shares profits)

A small co-invest helps align interests. Their brokerage license adds commissions on the purchase, the eventual sale, or the refinance.

**Lighter options.** They can earn a finder's or co-GP fee by bringing deals to larger sponsors, or use option agreements to control a property while they line up financing.

**Main risk: compliance.** As a licensed agent acting as principal, they must disclose their interest and avoid conflicts with clients. Raising passive money falls under securities law, typically a Regulation D 506(b) or 506(c) offering with proper counsel. Some states also restrict wholesaling by unlicensed people. Ignoring these rules can wipe out the gains.

The response describes sourcing, rehab, and lease-up as duties of a joint venture or syndication sponsor and mentions commissions separately, leaving the turnkey buyer service unaddressed.

The assignment and referral fees pay for transferring or sourcing deals, while the rehab management fees are presented as sponsor compensation rather than fixed project fees for executing rehabs without ownership.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: A broker-operator without acquisition capital can monetize undervalued distressed multifamily deals by pairing deal control and execution with outside capital. The most lucrative path is sponsoring a syndication or joint venture as the operating general partner while limited partners or an equity partner fund the purchase and renovations. In that structure, the operator earns acquisition, construction management, and ongoing asset or property management fees, alongside a promoted equity stake in cash flow and refinance or sale proceeds—often rolling their brokerage commission in as co-investment equity to align interests. If they prefer not to sponsor the debt or sign loan guarantees, they can bring the tied-up deal to an established sponsor as a co-GP for a share of fees and upside, or assign the purchase contract for a wholesale fee. Alternatively, they can broker the acquisition to a well-capitalized investor and lock in a long-term rehab management, property management, and future disposition agreement.

A broker-operator can earn cash at closing by bringing an undervalued apartment deal to a well-capitalized buyer and collecting an agreed brokerage commission. If they already control the property under a purchase contract that permits assignment, they can sell their contract rights to the buyer for an assignment fee.

For longer-term upside, they can partner with an investor who funds the acquisition, rehab, and reserves. The broker-operator contributes the deal and runs the renovation and lease-up. They can negotiate a rehab oversight or asset management fee and a share of profits, often payable after the investor gets its capital back and earns a preferred return.

To attract buyers or partners, show the purchase price, rehab budget, rent comps, and how returns change if costs rise or lease-up takes longer. Disclose any ownership interest and compensation, and check state licensing and wholesaling rules before marketing the deal or combining fees.

A broker-operator can bring the deal to an investor who can fund the purchase and rehab. The simplest route is to broker the sale and earn a commission at closing. For more upside, the operator can form a joint venture in which the investor supplies the capital and the operator finds the property, manages the renovation, and oversees leasing. The operator can negotiate fees for that work and a share of profits after the investor recovers its capital and earns an agreed preferred return.

If the operator already controls the property under an assignable purchase contract, they can transfer the contract to a buyer for an assignment fee. Whichever route they choose, they should support the valuation with comparable sales, a realistic rehab budget, and projected net operating income after stabilization, and disclose their role, compensation, and any conflicts of interest.
